blocks.text: Whiplash describes an acceleration-deceleration injury to the neck, most often from a rear-end or side-impact car crash. The resulting symptoms are called whiplash-associated disorders (WAD). The neck is forced rapidly into an S-shaped curve and then extension. Muscles, facet joints, ligaments and discs may be strained, but in most patients no specific damaged structure can be identified with imaging. Most people recover within weeks to months, but a meaningful proportion develop persistent pain and disability [Ref – to verify]. Persistent WAD is often linked to high initial pain, high initial disability, and signs of sensitisation and post-traumatic stress [Ref – to verify].

rows: Any high-risk factor? Age 65 or over, dangerous mechanism, or tingling in the limbs
Yes: imaging required. Immobilise and refer

Any low-risk factor that allows safe range testing? Simple rear-end collision, sitting in the emergency department, walking at any time since the injury, delayed onset of neck pain, no midline tenderness

No: imaging required. Yes: no imaging needed

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Midline bony tenderness, high-risk mechanism, age 65 or over, limb paraesthesia after trauma
Immobilise; do not move the neck; imaging
Bilateral limb symptoms, gait disturbance, bladder change
Dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, drop attacks, nystagmus, numbness of the face
Loss of consciousness, worsening headache, repeated vomiting, confusion

blocks.text: Defer: manipulation, end-range mobilisation and strong stretching until fracture, instability and vascular causes are excluded.

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

steps: **Trauma within 48 hours?** Apply the Canadian C-spine rule. Imaging needed: refer. Cleared: continue.
**Neurological signs?** Yes: grade III, radiculopathy pathway and monitoring.
**Vascular or head injury signs?** Yes: emergency.
**Neck pain with reduced range, tenderness, no neuro signs:** working diagnosis WAD grade II.
**Screen prognosis:** high pain (7/10 or more), high NDI, post-traumatic stress, widespread sensitivity point to risk of persistence. Address early.
**Start education and active exercise.** Reassess in 2 to 3 weeks.

rows: Gentle cervical and thoracic mobilisation (Maitland grades I to II early, III later)
Short-term pain relief and confidence in movement
Painful, limited segmental movement after fracture is excluded
Supine or sitting; small rhythmic oscillations within comfort
Short-term relief of neck pain [Ref – to verify]
Supine or sitting thrust after consent

blocks.text: Preferred starting choice: education plus active exercise. Manual therapy is an adjunct, not the main treatment. Avoid passive-only care that teaches the patient to depend on the therapist.

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

rows: Slow rotation, side flexion, flexion, extension within comfort
Supine nod, pressure biofeedback at the stage held well
Band rows with shoulder blades drawn back and down
Gaze stability and JPE training (if dizzy)
Relocate head to target with eyes closed; keep eyes on target while turning head

blocks.text: Symptom rule: mild increase during exercise that settles within a few hours is acceptable.

rows: Prolonged immobilisation delays recovery [Ref – to verify]
No meaningful benefit shown [Ref – to verify]

Subacute (2 to 12 weeks): progressive exercise, motor control, sensorimotor training, gradual return to driving and work.
Persistent (over 12 weeks): combine exercise with pain education, sleep and stress management; refer for psychological care if post-traumatic stress features are present.

blocks.text: Record NDI, pain 0 to 10, active rotation range, CCFT stage, and dizziness or JPE if relevant. Poor progress at 6 to 12 weeks with high distress should trigger a multidisciplinary approach.

blocks.label: CLINICAL CASE
body: A 29-year-old woman was rear-ended at low speed 3 days ago. She walked at the scene. Neck pain started the next morning, 6/10, rotation limited to about 50 degrees each side. No midline tenderness, no limb symptoms, no dizziness. She fears she has "damaged a disc". Working diagnosis: WAD grade II. Plan: reassurance, explain that most people recover, active range exercises, CCFT training, gradual return to work and driving.

items: **Does she need imaging under the Canadian C-spine rule?** No. No high-risk factor; low-risk factors present; she can rotate 45 degrees each way.
**Why avoid a soft collar?** Immobilisation is associated with slower recovery; active movement is preferred.
**What would change her grade to III?** Neurological signs such as reduced reflexes, weakness or sensory loss.
**Which factors would make you worry about a slow recovery?** High pain intensity, high NDI, post-traumatic stress symptoms and widespread sensitivity.
**She becomes dizzy with double vision during treatment. What do you do?** Stop immediately, treat as a possible vascular event and arrange emergency care.
Initial approach: screen with the Canadian C-spine rule, then reassure and activate.
Priority: early movement and confidence.
Manual therapy: adjunct only.
Exercise: range, deep neck flexor training, sensorimotor training if dizzy.
Modalities: limited; no collar.
Tell the patient: most people recover; movement is safe and helpful.
Avoid: immobilisation, passive-only care, alarming language.
Referral triggers: Section G and persistent high distress.
